questions.q: What does RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) mean?
options: Resources should always be allocated on the heap
A resource is acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor, so cleanup happens automatically when the object's scope ends
All resources must be released manually before a function returns
A resource can only be released by calling a global cleanup function
questions.explain: RAII ties a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime: acquire it in the constructor, release it in the destructor, which C++ guarantees runs deterministically when the object goes out of scope.

questions.q: Why can't a std::unique_ptr be copied?
options: Because the compiler doesn't support copying any class type
Because it represents exclusive ownership — copying it would create two owners of the same object, which it's designed to prevent
Because unique_ptr only works with int and double
Because copying a unique_ptr would make it a shared_ptr automatically
questions.explain: std::unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership of its managed object. Allowing copies would mean two unique_ptr instances both believing they own (and will delete) the same object — so copying is disabled; only moving is allowed.

questions.q: In `auto order1 = std::make_shared<Order>(...); auto order2 = order1;`, when is the Order actually destroyed?
options: Immediately when order2 is created
Only when order1 goes out of scope, regardless of order2
When the last shared_ptr owning it (whichever of order1 or order2 goes out of scope last) is destroyed or reset
Never automatically — shared_ptr requires a manual delete
questions.explain: std::shared_ptr uses reference counting: the managed object is destroyed only when the last shared_ptr referring to it is destroyed or reset, not when any particular one of them goes away.

questions.q: Why is std::make_unique<T>(...) generally preferred over calling `new T(...)` directly?
options: make_unique runs faster at runtime than new
make_unique is more exception-safe and slightly more concise, and avoids writing new/delete by hand
new is deprecated and no longer compiles in C++17/20
make_unique allocates on the stack instead of the heap
questions.explain: make_unique wraps allocation and ownership transfer in one exception-safe expression, and keeps you from needing to pair a raw new with a matching delete.

questions.q: According to this lesson's rules of thumb, when should std::shared_ptr be used instead of std::unique_ptr?
options: Always — shared_ptr should be the default smart pointer
Only when ownership of the object genuinely needs to be shared among multiple independent owners
Whenever the object is larger than 8 bytes
Never — shared_ptr should be avoided entirely in modern C++
questions.explain: unique_ptr should be the default because it has zero overhead versus a raw pointer. shared_ptr carries reference-counting overhead, so it's reserved for cases where ownership is genuinely shared, not used as a default convenience.
